ideas.title: The AI Earnings Supercycle Was Partly a Mark-Up
ideas.trend: Alphabet and Amazon Q1 earnings are dominating tech/investing Twitter this week, with coverage crediting AI monetization — but the Anthropic stake paper-gain story is gaining traction in fintech and investing circles
ideas.consensus: Google and Amazon had blowout AI quarters proving the hyperscaler capex thesis at scale
ideas.angle: Roughly $45B of those combined profits were unrealized Anthropic stake mark-ups triggered by a funding round — a classic PE accounting mechanism running inside two of the most-watched public earnings events on Earth

content_pack.x_longform:
The best AI earnings season on record was substantially an accounting event.

Alphabet posted $62.6 billion in Q1 net income, up 81% year over year. Amazon posted $30.3 billion, its best first quarter in company history. Together those results drove headlines about AI monetization arriving, cloud demand proving out, and the hyperscaler bull thesis confirmed at scale.

Roughly $45 billion of those combined profits came from one source: both companies marking up the book value of their Anthropic stakes.

Alphabet's filing is explicit: $28.7 billion classified as unrealized gains on equity investments. Not Search. Not YouTube. Not Cloud. Not Waymo. An accounting adjustment triggered when Anthropic raised its Series G at a higher valuation. Amazon's release states it directly: $16.8 billion in pre-tax gains from Anthropic investments, sitting inside non-operating income, per The Next Web's reporting on the Q1 release. Neither company has sold a share.

Strip those gains. Alphabet's $62.6 billion quarter becomes $33.9 billion. Amazon's $30.3 billion falls to roughly $13.5 billion. Both remain strong businesses. Neither generates the same coverage.

This is how private equity has inflated reported earnings for decades. A portfolio company raises at a higher valuation. The existing investor marks its position to the new price. The gain flows through the income statement. The cash never moves. This cycle, that mechanism runs inside two of the most-watched quarterly reports on Earth, producing paper gains equivalent to what Meta plans to spend on AI infrastructure in a full year.

The circularity deserves attention. Google committed $10 billion in fresh cash to Anthropic in April, with up to $30 billion more possible, per TechCrunch. Amazon's original $8 billion stake is now marked above $70 billion on the company's own books. The valuation that produced both paper gains was substantially anchored by the same new capital Google and Amazon injected. The companies are marking their investments up against a valuation their own money helped set.

The underlying businesses are real. AWS grew 28% to $37.6 billion, the fastest expansion in 15 quarters. Google Cloud hit $12.3 billion, constrained by capacity rather than demand. SemiAnalysis estimates Google's seventh-generation TPU undercuts NVIDIA's GB200 rack by 44% in total cost of ownership. These are structural advantages. The paper gains inflated already strong quarters.

What happens when Anthropic's private funding trajectory changes matters. If Anthropic IPOs at a lower multiple than its last private round, both companies reverse those gains. The same income statement that showed $45 billion in paper profits would show a paper loss. Investors who priced Alphabet and Amazon stock on these earnings reports built part of that position on an assumption about one private company's next valuation.

Cisco sat at $555 billion in March 2000. WorldCom booked capacity contracts before customers could use the infrastructure. Both used accounting to make a cyclical event look structural. Both unraveled when the mechanism driving the headline number changed.

The AI cloud businesses are real. The $45 billion in Anthropic mark-ups will repeat only as long as Anthropic keeps raising at higher valuations. When that cadence stops, the operating lines carry the story alone.

content_pack.substack_draft:
$45 billion. That number is doing all the work in this story.

Alphabet and Amazon reported their best quarters in recent history last week. The coverage credited AI monetization, cloud momentum, and the hyperscaler thesis being vindicated. What sat inside both earnings releases, and what most coverage understated: roughly $45 billion of those combined profits came from marking up their Anthropic stakes after the company's latest funding round. Neither has sold a share. The cash never moved.

This is how private equity inflates reported earnings. A portfolio company raises at a higher valuation, the existing investor marks the position up, and the gain flows through the income statement. What is new is the scale and visibility. That accounting mechanism now runs inside two of the most widely read quarterly earnings events on Earth.

The underlying businesses are genuinely strong. AWS grew 28%. Google Cloud is capacity-constrained. I would not argue those trends are fabricated. What I am less certain about is whether most investors pricing Alphabet and Amazon stock on these results understood they were partly pricing an unrealized gain on a private stake neither company can easily exit. The AI earnings supercycle and the paper wealth cycle are running in parallel this quarter. I am not yet sure how long they stay correlated, or what happens to the headline earnings story when Anthropic stops raising at higher valuations.

ideas.title: OpenAI's CFO Doesn't Think the Company Is Ready for an IPO
ideas.trend: The Altman-Friar IPO timing split is widely discussed across tech and finance Twitter this week, framed as an internal disagreement — the structural revenue-vs-commitment argument underneath it is underreported
ideas.consensus: OpenAI is on a clear path to a 2026 IPO — $25B revenue and 910M users make it inevitable
ideas.angle: The CFO's concern is structural: $600B in forward capex commitments against $25B ARR is a 24x ratio that public markets have never priced at this scale, and the reporting systems to satisfy quarterly scrutiny do not yet exist

content_pack.x_longform:
Sarah Friar guided Square through its IPO. She is now OpenAI's CFO. She does not think the company is ready.

OpenAI hit $25 billion in annualized revenue this year. 910 million weekly active users. $840 billion private valuation. Sam Altman wants a Q4 2026 listing. Friar is pushing 2027, flagging a number that is harder to dismiss than the growth metrics: $600 billion in forward infrastructure commitments already booked.

The tension is a revenue model question. $25 billion ARR is remarkable. $600 billion in capital commitments is a different sentence. The ratio is 24x. Public investors buying a 2026 OpenAI IPO would be underwriting the gap.

Square went public at a $2.9 billion valuation with a testable model: transaction volume times take rate equals margin. OpenAI is targeting a $1 trillion valuation with a business that has never posted positive operating cash flow at scale. Consumer subscription. Enterprise API. Hardware. Operator licensing. Four bets, none yet dominant enough to anchor a public multiple.

Friar's second concern, per The Information, is the reporting infrastructure. 10-Ks. Quarterly segment margins. Audited controls. Those systems take longer to build than revenue takes to grow. OpenAI spent five years operating as a mission-driven nonprofit hybrid. Retrofitting that into a public-company cadence is an operational project, not just a legal one.

Friar was at Goldman Sachs during the last cycle when technology companies went public at multiples disconnected from near-term cash flows. The market spent years revising them downward.

The 2026 IPO will happen if the market is willing. Whether it should and whether it will are two different questions. OpenAI has never had to answer both at once.

content_pack.substack_draft:
Most people I talk to treat the OpenAI IPO as a timing question. The more I read about the Friar-Altman divide, the more I think it is a capital structure question.

Sam Altman wants to list in Q4 2026. CFO Sarah Friar is pushing for 2027, citing $600 billion in forward infrastructure commitments and questions about whether the company's financial reporting systems are ready for public scrutiny. The number that stopped me is the ratio. OpenAI has $25 billion in annualized revenue and $600 billion in committed spending ahead. That is 24x. Public markets have priced technology companies at very high revenue multiples before. They have rarely if ever priced a business where forward capital commitments outrun current revenue by 24x and the path to closing that gap runs through a product category still defining which revenue stream will be primary.

I am not arguing OpenAI should not go public. I am genuinely uncertain what the right public market framework is for a business with this revenue trajectory, this capex structure, and this many unresolved questions about where the core margin story lives. Friar guided Square through its IPO. She has seen what happens when those questions are answered before the S-1 opens, and what happens when they are not.

ideas.title: Anthropic Built the Most Capable Hacking Model Ever. Then Refused to Sell It.
ideas.trend: Anthropic Mythos and Project Glasswing are trending across AI and cybersecurity circles this week after the red team technical release
ideas.consensus: Mythos is a major AI capability advance and another win for Anthropic in the frontier model race
ideas.angle: This is the first frontier AI capability deliberately withheld from commercial release — every prior capability advance was monetized; restraint as a product decision has no precedent in the commercial AI industry

content_pack.x_longform:
The most powerful offensive security model ever built shipped this week as a research preview for select partners only. Anthropic decided Mythos is too dangerous to sell.

Per Anthropic's own red team release: Mythos fully autonomously found and exploited a 17-year-old remote code execution vulnerability in FreeBSD, writing a 20-gadget ROP chain to gain root access on any machine running NFS. No human in the loop. It then scanned every major operating system and browser and found thousands of high-severity vulnerabilities.

Every frontier capability before this one found a commercial home. Mythos became Project Glasswing instead. Anthropic committing $100 million in usage credits to let defenders harden critical software before models with similar capabilities spread.

When the model finds zero-days faster than elite human hackers, the lab ships a defensive program. The next lab to hit this capability threshold will face the same choice.

content_pack.substack_draft:
Every major AI lab operates on the same basic product logic: build the most capable model possible, then sell access to it. Capability creates the moat. Revenue validates the bet. The loop is self-reinforcing.

Anthropic built Mythos. It found zero-day vulnerabilities autonomously across every major operating system and browser. It fully exploited a 17-year-old remote code execution vulnerability in FreeBSD with no human in the loop, writing a 20-gadget ROP chain to gain root access. Then Anthropic decided not to sell it. Project Glasswing uses Mythos to harden critical infrastructure, committing $100 million in usage credits to defenders. The model does not have a pricing tier.

This is the first time I can recall a frontier AI capability being deliberately withheld from commercial release on the grounds that releasing it broadly would be net harmful. I find myself uncertain about what this precedent means over a longer horizon. If Mythos-class offense capability eventually arrives at labs with fewer constraints on deployment, the window Anthropic is trying to use for defense narrows considerably. The question I keep returning to is whether restraint at the frontier is a durable strategy, or a head start that closes once the capability spreads.
